newsitem.title: USA: CME hogs end up, gains pared after new highs set.
newsitem.headline: CME hogs end up, gains pared after new highs set.

text.p: CME hog futures closed higher but off best levels on profit taking, after October and February surged to new contract highs early. Pork bellies closed up sharply at day's highs on short covering ahead of the weekly CME storage report, traders said.

Hog futures posted a new contract high of 60.300 cents per lb in October and 79.175 cents in lean February on buying prompted by higher cash hog projections before slipping late. Futures ended 0.900 cent higher to 0.450 lower with October up most at 59.925 cents and December up 0.500 at 57.975 cents. Only distant December posted a loss.

Expectations are for packers to raise bids for hogs on a firmer undertone to most cash pork products and generally tight market-ready hog supplies. Hog marketings were seen thinning for the remainder of the week as farmers return to fieldwork that had been halted by rain, traders said.

Chuck Levitt, senior livestock analyst for Alaron Trading Corp, predicted that the rate of hog slaughter will be down this week which should provide support to the pork complex and in turn, encourage packer demand for hogs.
"I think when tomorrow rolls around and (packers) have some overall improvement in their cutout they are going to want the hogs and we will see a firmer (cash hog) market," Levitt said.

Expectations for reduced hog slaughter added to short support demand that developed in pork belly futures, traders in that pit said. The lower kill rate and expectations for a larger-than-year-ago net out-movement in CME out-of-town data sparked early demand that touched off buy stops.
Some traders said they looked for another surprise in the out-of-town report which keep futures at highs late.

Belly futures rallied sharply from the start, on their first day of the permanently expanded 3.000-cent-a-lb limit, and ended at day's highs, up 0.275 to 0.200 cent paced by February at 78.875 cents a lb.
After the close, CME reported a net movement of bellies out of warehouses outside Chicago of 2.423 million lbs, well above the high end of expectations of out 0.5 million to 1.5 million lbs.
"It's getting to look more like we may have lower stocks on November 1 than October 1 and that's sometimes the forerunner of some very bullish things," Levitt added.
